E1597.summary: In a passage quoted from Agrippa, the Sephiroth, glossed as Hochma, are that on which the ass's influence occultly depends.
E1597.body: Voice: Agrippa, as quoted. The ass's influence is said to depend occultly on the Sephiroth, glossed in the same breath: “Sephiroth, i.e., Hochma” [III.2 ¶64]. So the text equates Sephiroth with Hochma here; it does not explain either further.

E1598.summary: In a passage quoted from Paracelsus, the sequestatrix is that which gives each thing its form and essence; Atwood links it to the special part of Intellect.
E1598.body: Paracelsus is quoted: “that is the sequestatrix, which gives to every thing its form and essence” [III.1 ¶21]. In the same passage Atwood seems to call either this sequestatrix or the Separation the special part of Intellect. The text leaves unclear which of the two she means.

E1599.summary: Two serpents found everywhere on earth, a living male and a living female, to be understood spiritually and not bodily.
E1599.body: Voice: Cornelius Agrippa's ingenious disciple, as quoted. The two serpents are found everywhere on earth: “they are a living male and a living female (understand in relation to the spirit always without all corporeal allusion)” [III.1 ¶50]. The text itself instructs a spiritual reading, without any bodily reference.

E1600.summary: Servius, commenting on Virgil, is cited to support the point that the Bacchic rites served to purify souls.
E1600.body: Atwood cites Servius's comment on Virgil in support of her point that the Bacchic rites were meant to purify souls: “Libris patris sacra ad purgationem animarum pertinebant” [II.2 ¶5]. A rough rendering (ours, not the book's): the sacred rites of Father Liber pertained to the purification of souls. The claim rests on Atwood's own use of the line, not on our rendering.

E1601.summary: Atwood says the great principle of the number seven is a Rest from the ferment of the Vitalizing or Divine principles.
E1601.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): “The great principle of the number seven is a Rest” [APP ¶69]. This is a rest from the ferment of the Vitalizing or Divine principles.

E1602.summary: In Hermes, seven bodies of which gold is first; Atwood reads them as the inferior spheres of vitality in which the soul of gold moves.
E1602.body: Atwood cites Hermes: “there are seven bodies --- of which gold is the first, the most perfect, the king of them, and their head” [I.3 ¶58]. In a note she explains what the bodies stand for. The aim is to “perfect all the other seven bodies; i.e., to signify here, according to Hermes, the inferior spheres of vitality in which it moves” [I.3 n65]. So she identifies the seven bodies with the inferior spheres of vitality in which gold's soul moves.

E1603.summary: Atwood takes the seven letters as the necessary phases the material passes through, marked by color and quality.
E1603.body: Atwood takes the seven letters as the necessary phases the material passes through, distinguished by color and quality. She notes that writers name them differently: “some call them planets, others metals (for the radical life of the spirit is indeed mineral)” [I.3 n47].

E1604.summary: The period in which the principles are separated, during which a coction goes on amid flood, eclipse and confusion.
E1604.body: Atwood uses severation for the period in which the principles are separated: “during this period of the severation, a wonderful coction is described as going on” [III.1 ¶53]. In her account this period is marked by flood, eclipse and confusion.

E1605.summary: A solvent known only to philosophers; Atwood says Cleopatra dissolved her earring in it.
E1605.body: Atwood tells how Cleopatra dissolved her earring in “such a sharp vinegar as is only known to philosophers on the ground of nature” [I.1 ¶18]. The text gives it no further identification.

E1606.summary: The ‘allegoric’ siege of life, to which the Rational Light is raised and where it overcomes the stronghold of evil.
E1606.body: Atwood says the Rational Light “afterwards is raised to the allegoric siege of life” [III.4 ¶19], where it overcomes ‘the stronghold of evil’. The term is not explained further here.

E1607.summary: Atwood says an entrance into the Signature clears the understanding to know things in their roots.
E1607.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): an entrance into the Signature clears the understanding for “the knowledge of things in their roots” [APP ¶63]. The term is not defined further here.

E1608.summary: In Norton's Ordinal, the simperings of the Stone must be known until it can no more simper.
E1608.body: Voice: Norton's Ordinal, as quoted: “To know the simperings of our Stone, Till it may no more simper do, nor cease,” [IV.1 ¶12]. The verse apparently sets simmering against boiling. This is the reader's inference; the text does not state it.

E1609.summary: What Van Helmont was led to perceive in his dream-like vision.
E1609.body: Atwood says Van Helmont, in a dream-like vision, was “led along into a perception of the simple element of nature” [III.2 ¶17].

E1610.summary: Named as the one who preserved the Anaxagoras passage that Atwood cites.
E1610.body: Atwood names Simplicius as the one who preserved the Anaxagoras passage she uses [III.1 ¶21]. Nothing more is said of him.

E1611.summary: Translator of an Indian record (Asiatic Researches, vol. 1) that Atwood cites: all mental appearances except the First Cause are image or delusion.
E1611.body: Atwood cites Sir William Jones's translation of an Indian record (Asiatic Researches, vol. 1, p.241) as giving the same instruction: every mental appearance except the First Cause is image or delusion. The record says: “know that to be the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness” [II.3 ¶48; II.3 n51]. She uses it as agreeing with her own position.

E1612.summary: In Hermes, a kind of sulphur, identified with lions' and cats' claws.
E1612.body: Voice: Hermes, as quoted. Siretz is a sulphur: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20]. It is also identified with “the lions' and cats' claws, which is siretz” [I.3 ¶20]. The text gives no further plain meaning.

E1613.summary: Those Geber condemns next above the Covetous: they stay ignorant by choice and hinder others; Atwood calls their skepticism the mock ally of rational skepticism.
E1613.body: Atwood reports Geber's judgment: “next above the Covetous, Skeptics are condemned by Geber” [III.4 ¶12]. In her account they remain ignorant by choice and hinder others. She adds her own view that modern skeptics only ‘ape’ sound reason, and that their skepticism is the ‘mock ally’ of rational skepticism. She apparently shares Geber's condemnation.

E1614.summary: Hermes' Tabula Smaragdina, quoted in full as comprising the working principle and total subject of the art; Atwood calls it the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art.
E1614.body:
Atwood quotes the Tablet in full (as the Smaragdine Table, also spelled ‘Smagardine table’, or the Emerald Table). She treats it as containing the working principle and total subject of the art, and calls it the only Egyptian remnant of the Sacred Art. Its key line: “that which is above is as that which is below” [I.1 ¶3; I.1 ¶7–10]. She endorses it and uses it repeatedly:

- As the Emerald Table, to show that agent and patient are one after dissolution, the One Thing: “That which is below is as that which is above” [I.2 ¶48].
- As the Smagardine Table, to show that both the spiritual agent and the spiritual patient must be prepared: “That which is above is as that which is below, and that which is below is as that which is above” [III.1 ¶41].
- In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), for the point about earth or the residuum: “The power is integral if it be turned into earth” [APP ¶110].

E1615.summary: Cited from the Republic, Theaetus and Phaedrus for Wisdom generating truth, for the grades of initiation, and as the one who knew the Nothing that is Wisdom.
E1615.body:
Atwood draws on Socrates:

- From the Republic and Theaetus: Wisdom generates truth, perfects imperfect things and calls forth latent Intellections. “Wisdom is generative of truth and intellect” [II.1 ¶37].
- From the Phaedrus, as explained in a passage from Proclus: the ordered grades of initiation. “For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia” [II.4 ¶23]. He is also the narrator of Plato's ascent to Intelligible Beauty [II.4 ¶29].
- Atwood identifies the Wisdom with the Nothing that Socrates knew [IV.4 ¶27].

She uses all three in support of her own position.

E1616.summary: Sol or the Sun: hidden inwardly in the Stone, imprisoned until penetrated by the mercurial Spirit, partner of the Moon, and given to the reduced body as its soul.
E1616.body:
Several voices speak of Sol:

- Hermes, as quoted: the Stone's sun and beams lie hidden within it. “My Sol and my beams are most inward and secretly in me” [I.3 ¶37]. Sol is also said to ‘follow’ in the seven letters, but this is not explained.
- Atwood, explaining how Mercury acts on gold: “the formal virtue of Sol is sealed; his sulphur is imprisoned” [III.3 ¶30]. Sol is unaware of himself until the mercurial Spirit penetrates him; then he sends forth his Light.
- Atwood on the Sun as the Moon's partner in the work. Citing Plutarch, she says “the operations of the Sun are seen to resemble those strokes which by mere dint of strength and force bear down all before them” [III.1 ¶45]. In a passage from Boehme, Sol is given to the reduced body as its soul: “give it Sol, viz., the soul” [III.1 ¶48].
- The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, as quoted: the Lion devours and eclipses the bright Sun and brings him to greater perfection. The Sun is the Moon's brother and bridegroom; with her he is parent of the King, and he feeds a red King. “This Lyon maketh the Sun sith [fith] soone To be joined to hys Sister the Moone:” [III.1 ¶65]. ‘Sol’ appears in parallel positions in the same verse, but the text does not state that it is the same as the Sun.
- Pierce, the Black Monk, as quoted, lists Sol among the contents of the seed without explaining it: “In the which is alle, Sol, Lune, Life and Light” [III.4 ¶21].
- Eirenaeus, as quoted, pairs Sol and Lune as the products of projection: “Most perfect Sol and Lune from fire receive” and “Innumerable parts to Sol’s estate.” [IV.3 ¶25]. Their effect will prove ‘both gold and silver pure’.

E1617.summary: Atwood equates the Sol principle with the vortex of life, to which Mars/Venus natures are drawn closely in consciousness.
E1617.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), equates the two: “the vortex of life ---the Sol principle” [APP ¶113]. Mars/Venus natures are drawn closely to it in consciousness.

E1618.summary: In Flamel, two Mercuries, one planted in the other, cherished in the Alembic over a constant sun-like fire.
E1618.body: Voice: Flamel, as quoted. He speaks of “the Solar and Lunar Mercury, and the plantation of the one in the other” [IV.1 ¶41]. Both are cherished in the Alembic over a constant fire like the sun's. The text does not explain this further.

E1619.summary: Light that the ethereal humidity nourishes and educates; set beside Sol as the source of all heat.
E1619.body: Atwood says the ethereal humidity “nourishes the Solar Light and educates it” [IV.1 ¶29]. In the same passage she sets the Solar Light beside Sol as the source of all heat.

E1620.summary: In the Mystere de la Croix, a solar sulphur or living philosophic gold, drawn by subtle operations from the vitriol left after Mars and Venus are conjoined.
E1620.body: Voice: the Mystere de la Croix, as quoted. After Mars and Venus are conjoined, subtle operations draw from the leftover vitriol “un souphre solaire ou or philosophique vivant” [III.3 ¶11]. Our rendering, not the book's: a solar sulphur or living philosophic gold. The phrasing equates solar sulphur with living philosophic gold.

E1621.summary: Atwood equates the Solar Tincture with the Aurific Light.
E1621.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer): “The Solar Tincture (Tinctura Solaris) is the Aurific Light.” [APP ¶92]. The term is not explained further.

E1622.summary: The wise king, cited throughout as a voice on Wisdom: its nature, its gift from above, its increase, and seeing all things in its Spirit.
E1622.body:
Atwood often cites Solomon, also called the wise king, in support of her own view of Wisdom:

- Wisdom of Solomon, chap. 7: a panegyric of Wisdom as pure, all-pervading and renewing, entering holy souls. “Wisdom, says the wise king, is more moving than any motion” [II.1 ¶44; II.1 n42].
- Wisdom of Solomon 8: 9: knowledge of creation comes by Conscious Intuition, taught by Wisdom. “For Wisdom, which is the Worker of all things, taught me.” [III.3 ¶49; III.3 n34].
- Wisdom of Solomon, 21: Wisdom must be given from above, and it preserves the righteous. “Or what man is he, asks Solomon, that can know the counsel of God?” [IV.3 ¶39; IV.3 n18].
- Atwood reads “the fear of God is the beginning of Wisdom” [II.3 ¶37] as the awe of the soul perceiving itself in its source.
- Proverbs iv, 8, 9 illustrates the increase of the fermenting light: “Exalt her, and she shall promote thee” [I.3 n45].
- Proverbs 24, 27 and Eccles. 4: Wisdom joined with strength, and two are better than one. “A wise man is strong, says the wise king, and knowledge increaseth strength” [III.1 ¶45; III.1 n51].
- The ‘enclosed garden of Solomon’ and the sealed fountain are identified with Elysium [II.4 ¶9].

Others cite him within passages she quotes:

- Charnocke's verse on the faithful servant: “A good servant, saith Solomon, let him be unto thee, As thine own hearte,in each degree” [III.4 ¶35].
- Eirenaeus, against idleness: “The desire of the idle shall cause him to perish” [IV.1 ¶6].
- Helmont, on the physician as created by the Lord: “Honor the physician with the honor due unto him” [IV.3 ¶34].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Solomon illustrates seeing the nature and virtues of all things in the Spirit of Wisdom [APP ¶67]. He also supports not exceeding the capacity one is given: “Be not righteous overmuch” [APP ¶110].

E1623.summary: The dissolving that is the first work and foundation of the art: the body reduced to water or mercury; for Atwood, also the separation of the sensuous medium and a converting comprehension.
E1623.body:
Friar Bacon and the Rosarium, as quoted, call Solution the first work: the body is reduced into water, that is, mercury, and “this is called Solution, which is the foundation of the whole art” [I.2 ¶5].

Atwood's own uses:

- She glosses the verb directly: “solve, that is comprehend, it on its own ground” [II.2 ¶15]. The impure perceptive medium needs this: “it needs alternation and solution, as the oracles teach” [II.2 ¶15]. And “The first rule of the work is a perfect solution” [II.2 ¶16].
- On the operation itself: “Solution dissolves and liquifies the included Spirit” [III.2 ¶64].
- Lully dissolved the Philosophic Salt: “he performed the Solution in nine days” [IV.1 ¶36].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer):

- Solution is both the answer to a question and a dissolving that enters and converts the enquirer, as light dissolves darkness: “every solution is a convertive process and progress in entity and hypostatic relation” [APP ¶115].
- Past the phantasmagoric region one is to “enter into its solution, i.e., in its dissolved essence” [APP ¶144], the world's dissolved essence.
- “Solution refers to the separation of the sensuous medium itself.” [APP ¶176]. This separation is repeated on the intuitional or medial life to reach the divine.

E1624.summary: A formula closing a verse on the fixed and the volatile, linked there to the inversion of fixed and volatile.
E1624.body: A verse on the fixed and the volatile closes with this formula: “Solve, Coagula, Fige.” [I.2 ¶21]. Our rendering, not the book's: dissolve, coagulate, fix. The passage ties it to the inversion of fixed and volatile. The voice is unclear from the text.

E1625.summary: Unnamed modern Kabalists whom Atwood cites to explain the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether.
E1625.body: Atwood cites some modern Kabalists for their explanation of the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether as “an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity” [III.2 ¶13].

E1626.summary: In Hermes, the son of king and red daughter, who takes his tincture from the fire and bears the Philosophic Matter: the whole quintessential nature concentrated and personified.
E1626.body:
Voice: Hermes, as quoted. The son is conceived of the king and the red daughter and takes his tincture from the fire. He is the whole quintessential nature concentrated and personified: “this son is himself the treasury, even himself bearing the Philosophic Matter” [I.3 ¶35].

Voice: the Master, as quoted. The Son is dead and then lives: “The Dragon shuns the sunbeams which dart through the crevices, our dead Son lives.” [IV.2 ¶14]. He takes his Tincture from fire and death, comes forth from the Fire, rejoices with his spouse, becomes a warrior in the Fire, and bears the Philosophic Matter. The same passage gives two identities: “Our Son the King” and “For this Son is the treasury” [IV.2 ¶14].
